title: Geospatial Indexing and Proximity Search
summary: Answer 'what is near me' with geohash, quadtrees, S2/H3 cells or PostGIS, ring-expansion search and in-memory indexes for moving objects.
body:
"Find drivers within 2 km", "restaurants near me", "friends on the map": proximity queries show up in ride-hailing, delivery, local search and dating designs. The interviewer wants to see that you know why an ordinary index struggles, which spatial index fits static points versus constantly moving ones, and how a nearby query actually executes. The core idea in every approach is the same: map two-dimensional locations onto one-dimensional keys or cells that an index can range-scan, then filter candidates by exact distance.

## Why a latitude/longitude B-tree fails

Put a composite B-tree index on `(lat, lng)` and query a box around a point. The index can seek to the latitude range, but within that range rows are ordered by latitude first, so the longitude condition cannot narrow the scan. You read a thin band of latitude that wraps the entire globe and discard almost all of it. Two separate indexes are no better: the database picks one and filters, or intersects two large ID sets. Circular radius queries, the antimeridian at 180 degrees and the fact that a degree of longitude shrinks toward the poles (about 111 km at the equator, about 79 km at 45 degrees latitude) make naive math worse. You need an index that keeps nearby points near each other.

## Geohash: a space-filling string

A **geohash** recursively halves longitude and latitude, interleaving one bit from each, and encodes the bits in base32 (5 bits per character). Each extra character subdivides the cell into 32 smaller cells, so points sharing a long prefix are close together. A 5-character geohash is about 4.9 km by 4.9 km, 6 characters about 1.2 km by 0.6 km, and 7 characters about 153 m by 153 m. Because the result is a string, an ordinary B-tree or a sorted set can answer "everything with prefix `9q8yy`" as a range scan.

The catch is edges. Two points a few metres apart on either side of a cell boundary can have completely different prefixes. The fix is to always query the target cell **and its 8 neighbours**, then filter by real distance. Redis GEO uses this approach internally: `GEOADD` stores a 52-bit geohash as the score in a sorted set, and `GEOSEARCH ... BYRADIUS` checks the neighbouring cell ranges and filters by distance.

## Quadtrees: adapt to density

A **quadtree** starts with one box covering the map and splits any node holding more than a threshold (say 100 points) into four quadrants. Dense downtown areas end up deeply subdivided while oceans stay as a single leaf, so every leaf holds a similar number of points.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    R["World: 4,000 points, split"] --> NW["NW: 30 points, leaf"]
    R --> NE["NE: 3,900 points, split"]
    R --> SW["SW: 40 points, leaf"]
    R --> SE["SE: 30 points, leaf"]
    NE --> A["NE-NW: 90, leaf"]
    NE --> B["NE-NE: 3,700, split further"]
    NE --> C["NE-SW: 60, leaf"]
    NE --> D["NE-SE: 50, leaf"]
```

The root splits because it exceeds the threshold; three quadrants are sparse and remain leaves, while the north-east quadrant, which contains a city, keeps splitting. A nearby search descends to the leaf containing the query point and checks adjacent leaves. Quadtrees are typically in-memory structures rebuilt periodically, which suits mostly static data such as business listings. Frequent updates make rebalancing (splitting and merging nodes) the bottleneck. The R-tree is the related structure most databases use: PostGIS builds R-tree-style GiST indexes over bounding boxes.

## S2 and H3 cells

Production systems at scale tend to use hierarchical cell libraries.

- **S2** (Google) projects the sphere onto the six faces of a cube and orders cells along a Hilbert curve, giving 64-bit cell IDs at 31 levels (0 to 30). Hilbert ordering keeps nearby cells numerically close better than geohash's Z-order, and S2 can cover an arbitrary region with a small set of cell ID ranges.
- **H3** (Uber) tiles the globe with hexagons at 16 resolutions (0 to 15). Every hexagon has six neighbours at the same distance, which makes "expand by one ring" uniform, and it suits aggregation such as surge pricing per cell. Resolution 9 cells average roughly 0.1 square kilometres. Hexagons do not nest perfectly between resolutions, so parent-child roll-ups are approximate.

| Approach | Best for | Strength | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Geohash in B-tree or Redis sorted set | Simple proximity on static or moderate data | Plain strings and range scans, easy sharding by prefix | Edge effects, uneven cell sizes by latitude |
| Quadtree (in memory) | Very uneven density, mostly static points | Leaves sized by density | Rebalancing cost under frequent updates |
| PostGIS (GiST on geography) | Rich queries: polygons, routes, joins | `ST_DWithin`, exact geodesic math, SQL | Single primary for writes; high update rates hurt |
| S2 / H3 cells | Large-scale services, aggregation, coverage | Uniform IDs, rings, region covering | Library dependency, choosing resolution |
| Redis GEO | Fast nearby on in-memory data | `GEOSEARCH` in milliseconds | Memory bound; one key per region to shard |

## The nearby search algorithm

Whatever the index, the query follows the same shape: convert the point to a cell, gather candidates from that cell and a ring of neighbours, compute exact distance, and expand if there are not enough results.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["Query: lat, lng, want K, max radius"] --> C["Find cell at chosen resolution"]
    C --> R["k = 1: fetch cell plus ring of neighbours"]
    R --> F["Compute exact distance, drop out of radius"]
    F --> E{"At least K results?"}
    E -->|"yes"| O["Sort by distance, return top K"]
    E -->|"no"| M{"Ring radius past max?"}
    M -->|"no"| X["k = k + 1: fetch next ring"]
    X --> F
    M -->|"yes"| O
```

Start at a resolution where one cell roughly matches the typical search radius. Fetch the cell plus its first ring, filter by the haversine or geodesic distance, and stop when you have K results whose distance is no larger than the inner radius of the rings covered so far; otherwise widen one ring at a time up to a maximum. Without that check, a result found in ring 1 can be farther away than an unchecked point in ring 2. Ring expansion handles both dense cities (stop after one ring) and rural areas (expand several times) without a fixed radius. For "top restaurants nearby", rank the candidates by a blend of distance and rating after the spatial filter.

## Moving objects

Drivers and couriers are the hard case. With 1 million active drivers each reporting every 4 seconds, that is 250,000 location writes per second, and most are overwritten seconds later. Writing each into a GiST index on a relational primary will not keep up and wastes durability on data with a short shelf life.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    DR["Driver apps: ping every 4 s"] --> GW["Location ingest service"]
    GW --> K[["Location stream partitioned by city"]]
    K --> IDX["Geo index shards: cell to driver set, TTL"]
    K --> HIST[("Trip history store")]
    RID["Rider: find nearby"] --> MS["Matching service"]
    MS --> IDX
```

Pings go through a stream partitioned by region, then into in-memory geo index shards (Redis GEO, or a custom map from H3 or S2 cell to the set of drivers in it). On each update the shard removes the driver from the old cell and adds it to the new one; entries expire if a driver stops reporting for, say, 30 seconds, so a crashed phone does not leave a ghost car. A separate consumer writes sampled history for trips and analytics. Sharding by city or region works because queries are local, but border areas need to query two shards, and a single dense city can need sub-partitioning by cell. Accept that the index is a few seconds stale; the matching step confirms availability with the driver before committing a trip.

## Common interview mistakes

- Using a `(lat, lng)` B-tree and calling it a spatial index.
- Querying only the containing geohash cell and missing neighbours across a boundary.
- Treating cell membership as distance; always filter by exact distance.
- Putting high-frequency location updates into a durable relational index.
- Ignoring stale entries from offline drivers.

## How to use it in an interview

Separate the two workloads: "Restaurants change rarely, so PostGIS or a geohash index in the main database is fine. Drivers move constantly, so their locations live in an in-memory geo index sharded by region with a TTL." Quote the update rate and the search radius, pick a cell resolution to match, and describe ring expansion. Expect follow-ups on hot regions (stadium at the end of a concert), the boundary problem, consistency between the index and the driver's real state, and memory sizing (1 million drivers at about 100 bytes each is around 100 MB per replica, which is small).

## Interview exercise

Design "find the 10 nearest available scooters" for 300,000 scooters across 50 cities, each reporting every 10 seconds. Choose an index, a cell resolution and a sharding key, estimate write throughput and memory, and walk through a query from a rider in a sparse suburb where the first ring is empty.

## Further reading

- [PostGIS documentation](https://postgis.net/documentation/) covers spatial indexes and `ST_DWithin`.
- [Redis GEOSEARCH command](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/geosearch/) documents radius and box queries over sorted sets.
- [H3 documentation](https://h3geo.org/docs/) explains hexagonal resolutions and grid rings.
keyTakeaways: A composite latitude/longitude B-tree can only narrow one dimension, so it scans a band around the globe.
Spatial indexes map 2D points to cells or 1D keys; always check neighbouring cells and filter by exact distance.
Quadtrees adapt to density for static data; S2 and H3 give uniform cell IDs and rings at scale.
Nearby search expands ring by ring until it has K results within the covered radius.
Frequently moving objects belong in a sharded in-memory geo index with TTLs, not a durable relational index.
